title: Asking without ordering
goal: Building commands, requests, and prohibitions at two levels of politeness — and knowing when a command actually sounds warm, not rude.
bekal: make commands for ته and for تاسو
forbid with مه, not with نه
soften requests with لطفاً، مهرباني وکړئ، او که کېږي

dialogs.title: خبرې اترې — په ټکسي کې
dialogs.intro: Budi takes a taxi on his own for the first time. The driver is friendly, the road is jammed, and every sentence has to come out right.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: سلام. مهرباني وکړئ، ما ته د پوهنتون خوا ته ولاړ شئ.
lines.baca: salām. mihrabānī wə́kṛəy, mā ta də pohantūn khwā ta wlāṛ shəy.
lines.id: Hello. Please take me toward the university.
lines.literal: greetings. kindness do-you, me to of university direction to going become-you.

lines.speaker: ډرایور:
lines.id: Sure, have a seat. Which gate?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: لومړۍ دروازه. که کېږي، ورو ولاړ شئ.
lines.baca: lūmṛəy darwāza. ka keẓī, wro wlāṛ shəy.
lines.id: The first gate. If possible, drive slowly.
lines.literal: first gate. if becomes, slow going become-you.

lines.speaker: ډرایور:
lines.text: هېڅ پروا نه لري. ټرافیک هرومرو ورو دی!
lines.baca: hets parwā nə larī. ṭrāfīk harūmarū wro day!

lines.speaker: ډرایور:
lines.id: There you go. It's hot today.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: لطفاً دلته مه دریږئ — لږ مخ ته ولاړ شئ.
lines.baca: lutfan dəlta ma dareẓəy — ləẓ makh ta wlāṛ shəy.

lines.literal: please here don't stop-you — a-little forward to going become-you.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: هلته، د جومات مخې ته. همدلته ودرېږئ.
lines.baca: halta, də jumāt makhe ta. hamdəlta wədareẓəy.

notes: Pashto commands **don't sound rude** the way bare commands can in English. کېنئ (sit) is a perfectly polite way to invite someone to sit down, and adding "please" in front actually sounds stiff. What makes it polite is the form for تاسو, not any extra word.
Note that commands always use the completed form with و- from unit 11: **و**کړئ، **وا**خلئ، **و**درېږئ. A command without و- means "keep on doing it", which is rarely what you mean.

⚠️ Prohibitions use **مه**, never نه. مه دریږئ means "don't stop"; نه دریږئ means "you don't stop" and isn't a prohibition at all. This mistake makes your sentence not just foreign-sounding but impossible to understand.

The most common softener is **مهرباني وکړئ**, literally "be kind". The Arabic word **لطفاً** is also widely used, especially in cities and in writing. The gentlest of all: **که کېږي**, literally "if it becomes", just like "if possible" in English.
The farewell blessing خدای دې مل شه means "may God be your companion". Pashto is full of short blessings like this, and they're not religious formality but everyday manners. Just answer مننه or آمین.
The phrase باقي پرېږدئ means "keep the change". Leaving the change as a tip is usual for taxi drivers but not for shopkeepers, and the amount is small — ten to twenty afghani is plenty.

grammars.title: Commands: two forms for two levels
body: The form for **تاسو** ends in ـئ, and it's what you use with almost everyone. The form for **ته** ends in ـه and is only used with close friends, younger siblings, and children.
Both forms take the completed prefix و-, and the stress falls on it. For verbs that refuse و- — راتلل، کېناستل، پاڅېدل — the command is made from the verb's own stem: راشئ، کېنئ، پاڅئ.

grammars.title: ⚠️ Prohibitions use مه
body: The form is the same as the command, just preceded by **مه** *ma*. The prefix و- may stay or drop, and both sound natural; what's required is the مه.
For a gentler prohibition, use a question-like form: **که کېږي، ونه کړئ** *ka keẓī, wə́-nə-kṛəy* — "if possible, please don't". This is the form used with older or more senior people.

sections.title: Request phrases for your first days

blocks.text: Pashto uses short blessings where English uses ordinary polite phrases. Learning them is the fastest way to sound like someone raised there, not like someone reading a phrasebook.

blocks.title: ⚠️ A greeting English doesn't have: ستړی مه شې
items: The phrase **ستړی مه شې** literally means "may you not get tired", and it's said to anyone at work: a builder, a driver, a tailor, a farmer, a teacher just out of class.
The reply is fixed too: **خدای دې ښه لره** *khudāy de ṣa lara* — "may God keep you well".
English has no equivalent, and that's exactly why it makes such an impression when you use it. To a woman, the form is ستړې مه شې.
Try it tomorrow on the first person you see working. The reaction will teach you more about Afghan culture than a chapter of a book.

blocks.title: Taking public transport in Kabul
items: Yellow taxis stop if you raise your hand. The fare is **always** agreed before you get in, not after: **پوهنتون ته څومره؟**
Minibuses are called **ملي بس** *millī bas* or **کاسټر** *kāsṭar*, and passengers say where to get off with **همدلته ودرېږه** *hamdəlta wədareẓa*.
To ask the driver to stop, the phrase isn't "stop" but **ودرېږئ** (stand). The verb درېدل means both to stand and to stop.
⚠️ Women usually sit in the back of a taxi, and that's expected. If you travel with a woman who isn't a relative, the rule applies to you too.

exercises.prompt: Make these into commands for تاسو.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: مه ځئ — مه دریږئ — مه خبرې کوئ — مه وېرېږه — مه خفه کېږئ
لطفاً ورو ووایئ. — لږ انتظار وکړئ. — ما سره مرسته وکړئ. — دلته مه دریږئ. — کېنئ.
مهرباني وکړئ، کړکۍ پرانیزئ. — لطفاً ورو ووایئ. — دلته مه دریږئ. — لږ انتظار وکړئ. — پوهنتون ته ولاړ شئ.
wave: Say ستړی مه شې tomorrow to the first person you see working, even if they don't understand Pashto. A sentence you only read fades; a sentence that has once left your mouth waits there until you need it.
